title: Iterator Pattern
subtitle: Provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.
keyTakeaways: Encapsulates collection traversal algorithms (Depth-First Search, Breadth-First Search, reverse order) away from the collection itself.
Allows multiple concurrent iterations over the same collection without modifying collection internal state.
The standard underpinning of Java's `java.util.Iterator`, `Iterable`, and the enhanced `for-each` loop.

sections.heading: Uniform Traversal without Breaking Internal Encapsulation
sections.body: Exposing internal collection structures (arrays, binary tree nodes, skip lists) to client code exposes private pointers and breaks encapsulation. The Iterator pattern provides a standardized cursor interface, allowing developers to switch from an array list to a balanced AVL tree without changing any client traversal loops.
bullets: Single Responsibility Principle: Traversal algorithms are extracted away from the data structure classes into dedicated iterator classes.
Open/Closed Principle: Introduce custom iterators (e.g., Breadth-First or Depth-First) without changing the data structure.
Fail-Fast Semantics: Modern iterators detect concurrent modifications using version counters (`modCount`), throwing `ConcurrentModificationException`.

tradeOffs.pros: Hides data structure representation; supports multiple simultaneous traversals; clean unified API.
tradeOffs.cons: Overkill for simple arrays where indexed `for` loops are marginally faster and simpler.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Complex graphs, binary trees, paginated database cursor streams.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero object allocation overhead; direct memory pointer access.
tradeOffs.cons: Tightly binds client to array indexing; fails for trees and linked graphs.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-performance primitives arrays in numerical computing.

interviewTip: In interviews, explain Java's Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe iterators: Fail-Fast (e.g. `ArrayList.iterator()`) throws `ConcurrentModificationException` if the underlying list changes during iteration. Fail-Safe (e.g. `CopyOnWriteArrayList`) operates on a clone of the collection and never throws.
